title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
text: The fact that I studied R led me to question how classroom programming stacks up against the technologies referred to in job advertisements. For a person looking into technology careers, would learning Python, web development, or cloud infrastructure be a useful next move? I collected two of the Hacker News “Who is hiring?” threads and then compared them using a fixed list of 20 technology categories. Python is mentioned in 27.7% of the hiring comments that remained from September 2026, which is the highest proportion among the categories in question, while I was surprised to find out that R appears in 0 of 256 postings. Python is a reasonable place to start for this kind of job. However, the analysis does not indicate which skill will yield the highest payoff or increase an individual’s chances of getting an offer.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
text:
Where the data comes from
The data comes from the September 2025 and September 2026 threads. The acquisition metadata were saved on 19 September 2026. I used an R scraper with rvest to collect public HTML, cache the pages, and wait 30 seconds between each new page request. The current robots.txt asks for this delay and allows access to /item. The workflow does not get around logins, paywalls, or CAPTCHAs. While Hacker News has an official API, I used HTML extraction to practice the rvest workflow required for this assignment. No new requests are needed to reproduce the saved analysis.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
text:
Turning comments into measurements
The files contain 863 comments, some of which are replies. I kept the top-level comments that include text, removed duplicate comment IDs, and excluded 10 entries identified during review as discussions, personal job-seeking or service offers, or insufficiently informative content. The final dataset consists of 294 hiring comments from 2025 and 256 from 2026. The IDs of the excluded entries together with the reasons for their exclusion are saved with the code. Each comment is counted only once even if it promotes more than one job; likewise, the same employer can be listed more than once.
Keyword matching also has to be checked. I only caught the “Go” bug because its count jumped from 26 to 42 between two runs on identical data, triggered by phrases like “Go for it” and “Go-To-Market”. Updating the matching rules resolved those false positives and captured the all-caps GO spelling. For the other options, the criteria are intentionally kept narrow: SQL counts the single term, while Postgres includes PostgreSQL. It is not appropriate to add the percentages since comments can refer to both. These adjustments cover mentions such as company technology stacks, not the verified requirements for each advertised role.


Show code
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "skill_share_2026.png"))








Figure 1: Leading technology categories in retained September 2026 hiring comments. Ties at rank 12 are included.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
section: What was the difference between the two snapshots?
text:
What was the difference between the two snapshots?
TypeScript and React make up 20.3% and 19.9% of the retained comments from 2026, respectively. Their proportions are 8.3 and 8.0 percentage points lower than in the 2025 snapshot. These are the observed differences, not an indication of a widespread decline in demand for web development.
Comparing two September threads eliminates one aspect of the seasonal mismatch by using the same calendar month, but it does not keep the hiring population constant. The September 2026 data was still incomplete at the time of collection, and each thread includes different employers and positions. Because this is a self-selecting online community, not a random selection of jobs, keyword rules may also miss abbreviations or count occasional references. For these reasons I give the comparison only a descriptive account rather than treating these differences as evidence about the wider labour market.


Show code
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "skill_change.png"))








Figure 2: Observed differences in mention shares across the two saved September threads. These are descriptive comparisons, not causal effects or population estimates.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
section: What is the right thing for a student to do in this situation?
text:
What is the right thing for a student to do in this situation?
If a student is already using R and wants to learn about the types of jobs listed here, I suggest they create a small Python project by obtaining data, cleaning it, and publishing a reproducible analysis. While Python is prominent, such a project should be seen as a reasonable experiment rather than a sure way to secure a job. Alternatively, a student aiming for a career in web development could build a TypeScript/React application, since both are still frequently mentioned even though they have lower proportions in this comparison.
Before you decide on a longer course, look at a selection of advertisements that correspond to your location, level of experience, and the position you want. Determine which technologies are essential and which only refer to the employer’s technology stack. This matters because the dataset includes senior engineering positions, junior ones, and non-technical roles. The lack of a verified R keyword match in this case does not prove that R is unimportant for jobs in economics or statistics.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
text:
In 2022, bringing inflation down raised an uncomfortable question. Would relief at the checkout come at the cost of more people losing work? Some prominent economists warned of a substantial rise in unemployment, while others thought inflation could ease without a painful recession. For households already struggling with rising bills, the possibility of losing a paycheck made the stakes especially high.
That debate makes the subsequent experience worth examining. Did the fall in U.S. inflation after 2022 come with a large rise in unemployment? And did that rise happen throughout the slowdown in inflation, or mainly toward the end?
One reason to expect a tradeoff is that strong spending can encourage hiring while also pushing prices up. Slowing spending could ease price pressure but weaken hiring. This is one idea behind the Phillips curve. It is a possibility to investigate, not a rule that the two rates must always follow.
Inflation measures how much prices increased compared with the same month a year earlier. Unemployment measures the share of people working or seeking work who have no job and are looking for one. Falling inflation means prices rise more slowly, not that prices fall.
The first chart shows why timing matters. Inflation peaked at 9.0% in June 2022 and fell sharply afterward. From that peak to December 2024, unemployment rose by 0.5 percentage points.








Figure 1: Inflation began falling before unemployment began its sustained rise.





That comparison misses an important turn along the way. Unemployment initially continued falling, reaching its low in April 2023. From that low to December 2024, it rose 0.7 points. Measuring from peak inflation therefore gives a smaller increase than measuring from the later unemployment low. The starting date changes how much weakening we see.
Was this simply a predictable exchange between inflation and jobs? The second chart checks whether similar unemployment consistently came with similar inflation. Each point represents one month, grouped into 2015 through 2019 before COVID, the disruption in 2020 and 2021, and the inflation and cooling period from 2022 through 2024.








Figure 2: Months with similar unemployment had very different inflation rates across the three periods.





Unemployment was 3.6% in December 2019 and 3.6% in June 2022. Yet inflation was 2.3% in the first month and 9.0% in the second. Similar unemployment accompanied very different inflation. Unemployment alone does not explain the price pressures households faced.
The final chart returns to the recent episode and connects the observations in time. Each point averages three months to make the path easier to follow. Moving downward means inflation fell; moving right means unemployment rose. Its unemployment axis is narrower than the previous chart’s, so distances should not be compared across the two figures.








Figure 3: The arrows trace an early fall in inflation followed by a clearer rise in unemployment.





Much of the initial movement was downward. From 2022 Q2 to 2023 Q2, inflation fell from 8.6% to 4.1%, while unemployment stayed close to 3.5%.
Afterward, the path moved more clearly to the right. By 2024 Q4, unemployment averaged 4.1% and inflation 2.7%. The broad contrast matters more than movements of a tenth of a point, since estimates from a sample of households can fluctuate even without a real change in unemployment.
The episode does not show a fixed exchange in which each point of lower inflation requires an equal rise in unemployment. It also does not establish that reducing inflation is always painless. The availability of goods, spending, expectations about future prices, and policy can all affect these outcomes. These charts cannot isolate the effects of a particular policy, and national averages conceal different experiences across households.
The main takeaways are:

Much of the fall in inflation came before the clearer rise in unemployment.
Unemployment rose by 0.5 percentage points from peak inflation, or 0.7 points from its subsequent low. The starting date matters.
Similar unemployment came with very different inflation, so unemployment alone does not explain price pressure.

Data come from BLS via FRED’s consumer price index and unemployment rate. The GitHub repository contains the data, code, methods, and instructions for reproducing the analysis.

title: Did lower inflation require much higher unemployment?
text:
Does bringing inflation down require a large increase in unemployment? The question matters because price stability and access to jobs both affect living standards. A simple inflation–unemployment trade-off suggests that a weaker labor market should accompany slower price growth. But a chart showing two variables moving together cannot establish how much unemployment a policy must create to reduce inflation.
I examine U.S. monthly data from 2015 through 2024, comparing the years before COVID, the disruption in 2020–2021, and inflation’s rise and retreat in 2022–2024. This fixed window provides a pre-pandemic benchmark and keeps the comparison separate from later developments. The central finding is that the relationship changed substantially across these periods.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
text:
Measuring the two rates
The data come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics through FRED. The series are CPIAUCSL, the all-items consumer price index, and UNRATE, the unemployment rate. Both series are seasonally adjusted. Unemployment measures unemployed people as a share of the civilian labor force, not the entire population.
I calculate inflation as 100 × (CPI this month / CPI twelve months earlier − 1). An extra year of CPI data supplies the initial comparison, leaving 120 matched monthly observations. This is a growth rate, rather than the CPI’s index level. Falling positive inflation means prices are increasing more slowly, not necessarily falling. Because the calculation uses seasonally adjusted CPI, it can differ slightly from the commonly reported year-over-year rate based on unadjusted CPI.

title: Did lower inflation require much higher unemployment?
text:
First, establish the sequence

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/timeline.png"))







Figure 1: Aligned monthly series with a common vertical scale. The unemployment spike precedes the inflation peak.





Figure 1 shows unemployment reaching 14.8% in April 2020, when inflation was only 0.3%. Inflation instead peaked at 9.0% in June 2022, with unemployment at 3.6%. These peaks describe different stages of the episode, rather than one simultaneous shock.
By December 2024, inflation was 2.9% and unemployment was 4.1%. Relative to the inflation peak, inflation declined 6.1 percentage points while unemployment rose 0.5 points. The endpoint comparison is striking, but the intervening path matters too.

title: Did lower inflation require much higher unemployment?
text:
Next, compare relationships across periods

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/scatter.png"))







Figure 2: Each point pairs inflation and unemployment in the same month. Period boundaries are descriptive calendar groupings, not estimated structural breaks.





Figure 2 shows why one fitted line would hide important differences. Before COVID, relatively low unemployment coexisted with modest inflation. During 2020–2021, high-unemployment months had low inflation, while inflation rose as unemployment receded. In 2022–2024, inflation varied widely within a much narrower unemployment range.
For a concrete comparison, unemployment was 3.6% in December 2019 and 3.6% in June 2022, but inflation was 2.3% and 9.0%, respectively. Unemployment alone does not summarize the inflation environment.

title: Did lower inflation require much higher unemployment?
text:
Finally, follow the disinflation path

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/path.png"))







Figure 3: Arrows connect consecutive quarters from 2022 through 2024. Both coordinates are averages of monthly rates; the horizontal scale is deliberately narrower than in Figure 2.





Figure 3 restores the time ordering lost in the scatterplot. Between 2022 Q2 and 2023 Q2, average inflation fell from 8.6% to 4.1%, while unemployment moved from 3.6% to 3.5%. Much of that initial disinflation occurred without rising unemployment. By 2024 Q4, unemployment had increased to 4.1%, with inflation at 2.7%. The later labor-market cooling should not be erased by focusing only on the earlier improvement.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
text:
Takeaway and limits
Much of the inflation decline preceded the clearer rise in unemployment. In Phillips curve terms, the observed path does not resemble a fixed exchange of one percentage point of unemployment for each point of lower inflation. This does not reject the broader Phillips curve framework. The unemployment increase is also larger when measured from its trough rather than from peak inflation.
These charts cannot identify a policy’s causal effect. Supply conditions, demand, expectations, and policy can all affect the relationship. National averages also conceal differences across workers and households. The finding describes this episode, not a universal rule about the cost of reducing inflation.
Data and replication. BLS via FRED, downloaded 2026-10-01. Observations reflect the saved download vintage, not information available in real time during the episode.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
text:
A low unemployment rate does not tell us whether people are participating in the labor market. Someone who stops looking for work generally leaves the unemployment-rate denominator. Labor-force participation asks a different question: what share of the population is working or looking for work? That distinction matters when comparing younger adults, people in their main working years, and older adults.
I analyze IPUMS CPS microdata in order to determine participation levels in 2024 relative to the levels in 2019. The overall annual participation rate decreased from 63.4% to 62.9%, which means that participation in 2024 was 0.5 percentage points lower than in 2019. The figures below present how that aggregate comparison relates to participation within age groups and changes in the population’s age mix.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
text:
A low unemployment rate does not tell us whether people are participating in the labor market. Someone who stops looking for work generally leaves the unemployment-rate denominator. Labor-force participation asks a different question: what share of the population is working or looking for work? That distinction matters when comparing younger adults, people in their main working years, and older adults.
I analyze IPUMS CPS microdata in order to determine participation levels in 2024 relative to the levels in 2019. The overall annual participation rate decreased from 63.4% to 62.9%, which means that participation in 2024 was 0.5 percentage points lower than in 2019. The figures below present how that aggregate comparison relates to participation within age groups and changes in the population’s age mix.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
text:
Measuring participation consistently
Labor-market participation is measured in a consistent way. The analysis includes all 72 Basic Monthly CPS samples from January 2019 through December 2024. It includes civilians age 16 or older with a defined labor-force status and a positive sampling weight. It includes March Basic but excludes the separate ASEC supplement.
For each month and age group, I divide the weighted number in the labor force by the weighted eligible population. I use WTFINL, the Basic Monthly person weight, so observations represent different numbers of people. LABFORCE identifies participation. Each annual estimate then averages the twelve monthly rates equally. These are descriptive, unadjusted estimates. IPUMS recommends COMPWT for replicating published BLS labor-force estimates; WTFINL is appropriate for most Basic Monthly analyses, so these rates need not match BLS headline figures.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
text:
First, compare recovery paths


Code
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "trends.png"))








Figure 1: Annual means of monthly weighted participation rates, expressed as changes from 2019. Panels use identical percentage-point scales; zero marks each group’s baseline.





Figure 1 shows changes from 2019 across four stages of working life. Among adults aged 25–54, participation was 82.7% in 2019 and 83.7% in 2024. For adults aged 65 and older, the corresponding estimates were 20.7% and 19.9%.
All four groups declined between 2019 and 2020. Ages 16–24 had the deepest decline (-2.4 percentage points), possibly reflecting disruption to entry-level work; their participation rebounded above baseline in 2023 before falling back toward it in 2024. Their subsequent paths diverged: participation among adults aged 25–54 exceeded its baseline by 2023, while the rate for adults aged 65 and older remained below it throughout 2020–2024. The shared change scale makes the declines and recovery paths visible, but gives up a direct comparison of participation levels. Figure 2 focuses on the final year.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
section: Next, compare changes against the same baseline
text:
Next, compare changes against the same baseline


Code
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "changes.png"))








Figure 2: Participation in 2024 minus participation in 2019. Zero indicates a return to the baseline annual rate.





Figure 2 plots each group on a common change metric. Adults aged 25 to 54 recorded the highest rise, roughly 1.0 percentage points. The age group 55–64 saw an increase of 0.7 points, while those aged 16–24 were approximately unchanged, gaining just 0.1 points. Adults aged 65 and older were the only group below their 2019 value, down by 0.8 points.
Thus, recovery was uneven. It would be inaccurate to say that all older adults had the same experience: for instance, the age group 55 to 64 exceeded its baseline while the group aged 65 and older did not. These comparisons describe outcomes, but they do not identify whether retirement, health, schooling, or care responsibilities caused the differences.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
section: Finally, hold the age mix fixed
text:
Finally, hold the age mix fixed


Code
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "age_mix.png"))








Figure 3: Overall participation changes, observed and standardized to 2019 age-group shares. Both series equal zero in 2019 by construction.





An overall rate combines each group’s participation rate with its population share. Figure 3 holds the four shares at their 2019 values for each calendar month while allowing participation within groups to change. Under that calculation, participation in 2024 was 0.4 percentage points higher than in 2019. The standardized 2024 level was 1.0 percentage point higher than the observed level.
Thus, the observed shortfall becomes a modest increase when the broad age mix is held fixed. A shift in population shares toward groups with lower participation can pull down the overall rate even when most groups improve. The roughly 1.0-point gap quantifies that composition effect under this particular standardization. It does not estimate what a policy would accomplish. Changes within these broad age bands remain, and the survey does not follow a fixed cohort for this analysis.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
text:
Takeaway and limits
By 2024, participation had surpassed its 2019 level for adults aged 25–64, approximately returned to it for younger adults, and remained lower for adults aged 65 and older. The aggregate shortfall therefore does not indicate a universal failure to recover. Population composition and age differences both matter.
The CPS has a complex rotating design, and pandemic-era collection disruptions complicate interpretation. I report descriptive differences without claiming causality or statistical significance. Annual averages also hide short-lived monthly changes.

Data: Flood et al. (2025), IPUMS CPS: Version 13.0, University of Minnesota. Basic Monthly samples, January 2019–December 2024; extract created September 27, 2026. The analysis uses 6,146,546 eligible person-month observations, not unique individuals.
Code and replication: Blog repository. The post folder contains the R analysis, aggregate results, figures, and replication instructions. Raw microdata are excluded from Git.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
Imagine reading a study that reports \(p=0.03\). Does that mean its conclusion has a 97% probability of being correct? No. Understanding why matters whenever we use statistical results to judge a policy, a business decision, or a scientific claim. The question this post answers is: what probability does a p-value actually measure, and what can we conclude from it?
This distinction is important enough that the American Statistical Association’s statement on p-values explicitly addresses it. A p-value does not give the probability that the tested hypothesis is true. To see what it does give, we need to separate two questions that sound similar.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
Imagine reading a study that reports \(p=0.03\). Does that mean its conclusion has a 97% probability of being correct? No. Understanding why matters whenever we use statistical results to judge a policy, a business decision, or a scientific claim. The question this post answers is: what probability does a p-value actually measure, and what can we conclude from it?
This distinction is important enough that the American Statistical Association’s statement on p-values explicitly addresses it. A p-value does not give the probability that the tested hypothesis is true. To see what it does give, we need to separate two questions that sound similar.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
section: Start with the direction of the question
text:
Start with the direction of the question
We often want to ask, “Given these results, how plausible is my hypothesis?” A significance test instead asks, “If the null model were correct, how often would results this extreme or more extreme occur?” The first question concerns the hypothesis after seeing the data; the second concerns possible data under an assumed hypothesis.
An analogy helps: knowing that a professional basketball player is likely to be tall does not tell us that a tall person is likely to be a professional basketball player. Reversing the condition changes the question. In statistics, a posterior probability such as \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\) requires a model for the alternatives and prior probabilities, not just a p-value.
We can make that distinction concrete by constructing a world where the null hypothesis is true from the outset.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
Build a simple null world
Suppose we observe 30 independent measurements on a standardized outcome and want to test whether its population mean is positive. Our hypothetical observed sample mean is 0.34. Assume the observations are normally distributed with a known standard deviation of 1. These are teaching assumptions, not data from an actual study.
The null hypothesis is \(H_0:\mu=0\), and the alternative is \(H_1:\mu>0\). Because we specify a positive direction in advance, this is a one-sided test. Its p-value is
\[
p=P(\bar X\geq 0.34\mid\mu=0,\text{ assumed sampling model}).
\]
Here, \(\bar X\) is the sample mean. Under the null, it varies around zero with standard deviation \(1/\sqrt{30}\). The p-value measures the right-tail probability beyond 0.34. It does not measure the probability of observing exactly 0.34 or the probability that \(\mu=0\).

title: What a p-value actually tells you
section: Use simulation to make the probability visible
text:
Use simulation to make the probability visible
The R code below repeats this hypothetical experiment 10,000 times. Each repetition draws 30 observations from the null model and records their mean. Counting the means at least as large as 0.34 approximates the probability in the equation. Simulation is useful here because it turns an abstract conditional probability into a fraction of repeated experiments.

set.seed(42)                 # Make the simulation reproducible.
n <- 30
obs_stat <- 0.34
repetitions <- 10000
null_stats <- replicate(repetitions, mean(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)))
p_sim <- mean(null_stats >= obs_stat)
p_exact <- pnorm(obs_stat, mean = 0, sd = 1 / sqrt(n), lower.tail = FALSE)
stopifnot(abs(p_sim - p_exact) < 5 * sqrt(p_exact * (1 - p_exact) / repetitions))

rnorm() generates observations, replicate() repeats the experiment, and the final mean() of the comparison counts the fraction meeting our threshold. pnorm() calculates the exact normal tail probability for comparison; it does not simulate another set of experiments.








Figure 1: Simulated sample means under the null (histogram), with their exact normal density (blue). The orange area under the curve is the exact one-sided p-value beyond the observed mean of 0.34.





The simulated fraction is 2.9%, close to the exact value of 3.13%. Thus, under our zero-mean model, about 3.1 in every 100 repetitions would produce a mean at least this large. The small difference between simulation and calculation is Monte Carlo variation. A two-sided test would also count equally extreme negative means and answer a different question.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
What should we conclude?
The observed mean is unusual under the specified null model, providing evidence against it. But every simulated experiment assumed the null was true: we never generated a mixture of true and false hypotheses. The simulation therefore cannot tell us what fraction of hypotheses are true after a small p-value appears.
Nor does a small p-value establish that an effect is economically important. Here, the estimated mean is 0.34 standardized units; its practical meaning depends on the outcome and context. Assumptions, uncertainty, study design, and whether the test was chosen before looking at the data also matter. A large p-value, conversely, would not prove that the mean is zero.
The takeaway is to read a p-value as a statement about results under a model. Report what was estimated and how uncertain it is, and resist translating \(p=0.03\) into “97% certain.” That translation answers a question the test never calculated.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
Reference
Wasserstein, R. L., and Lazar, N. A. (2016). The ASA’s Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose. The American Statistician, 70(2), pages 129 to 133.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
text:
U.S. inflation fell sharply after its 2022 peak, while unemployment increased much less. That comparison raises a specific question. How much did unemployment rise, and did it rise throughout the period when inflation was falling? The distinction matters because an endpoint comparison can hide when workers faced a weakening labor market.
I use monthly data from 2015 through 2024 to put the adjustment in context. The earlier years provide a benchmark for comparing similar unemployment rates under different inflation conditions. The main finding is that the adjustment occurred in two stages. Inflation initially declined substantially with little change in unemployment. Later, unemployment rose while inflation declined more slowly. These are descriptions of the observed path, not estimates of what a policy required or caused.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
section: When did inflation and unemployment turn?
text:
When did inflation and unemployment turn?
Before comparing the two rates directly, Figure 1 establishes their timing. The aligned panels let us see whether their peaks and declines occurred together.

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/timeline.png"))







Figure 1: Aligned monthly series with a common vertical scale. The unemployment spike precedes the inflation peak.





Figure 1 shows unemployment reaching 14.8% in April 2020, when inflation was only 0.3%. Inflation instead peaked at 9.0% in June 2022, with unemployment at 3.6%. The unemployment peak preceded the inflation peak, so treating the entire episode as one simultaneous movement would miss its sequence.
By December 2024, inflation was 2.9% and unemployment was 4.1%. Relative to the inflation peak, inflation declined 6.1 percentage points while unemployment rose 0.5 points. That endpoint comparison measures the overall movement. To understand it, we first need to ask whether the same unemployment rate has consistently been associated with similar inflation.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
section: Did similar unemployment mean similar inflation?
text:
Did similar unemployment mean similar inflation?
Those turning points invite a broader comparison. Figure 2 pairs the rates in each month, with colors and shapes separating 2015 through 2019 (before COVID), 2020 and 2021 (disruption), and 2022 through 2024 (inflation and cooling).








Figure 2: Each point represents one month. Calendar groups provide historical context and are not estimated structural breaks.





Unemployment was 3.6% in December 2019 and 3.6% in June 2022, but inflation was 2.3% and 9.0%, respectively. Similar unemployment did not imply similar inflation. This cautions against interpreting all the points as one stable relationship. The scatterplot, however, hides time ordering within each group, which the final chart restores.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
section: How did the adjustment unfold after 2022?
text:
How did the adjustment unfold after 2022?
Figure 3 reconnects observations in time order. I average each rate over three months to make the path easier to follow, at the cost of hiding monthly fluctuations. Downward movement means falling inflation, and rightward movement means rising unemployment. Arrows point toward the next quarter. The narrower horizontal scale makes small unemployment changes visible; distances should not be compared with Figure 2.

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/path.png"))







Figure 3: Arrows connect consecutive quarters from 2022 through 2024. Both coordinates are averages of monthly rates; the horizontal scale is deliberately narrower than in Figure 2.





Figure 3 restores the time ordering lost in the scatterplot. Between 2022 Q2 and 2023 Q2, average inflation fell from 8.6% to 4.1%, while unemployment moved from 3.6% to 3.5%. Much of that initial disinflation occurred without rising unemployment. By 2024 Q4, unemployment had increased to 4.1%, with inflation at 2.7%. From 2023 Q2 to 2024 Q4, unemployment rose 0.6 percentage points, while inflation fell a further 1.3 points. That later stage combined a clearer increase in unemployment with a slower decline in inflation.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
section: What the two stages tell us
text:
What the two stages tell us
The answer depends on the interval. From the monthly inflation peak to December 2024, unemployment rose 0.5 percentage points as inflation fell 6.1 points. The quarterly path reveals what that summary hides. Much of the initial inflation decline occurred with unemployment nearly unchanged, followed by a period of rising unemployment and smaller additional inflation declines.
This pattern does not establish that reducing inflation is always costless, or that a particular policy caused either movement. Supply conditions, demand, expectations, and policy may all matter, and these two series cannot separate their contributions. The calendar groups are descriptive, not estimated structural breaks. National averages also conceal differences between workers and households.
The central takeaway is specific to this episode. Falling inflation and rising unemployment did not move together at a constant pace. Looking at the sequence reveals both the early improvement and the later labor market weakening that an endpoint comparison alone misses.

Data and replication: BLS series distributed by FRED, downloaded 2026-10-01. These are revised historical observations, not real-time vintages. Code, saved data, and instructions reproduce all figures and reported numbers.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
text:
U.S. inflation fell sharply after its 2022 peak. How much did unemployment rise during that decline, and when? This question relates to the Phillips curve, which connects inflation and unemployment but does not establish a fixed policy tradeoff. For workers, an endpoint comparison can conceal whether a weakening labor market accompanied the entire adjustment or only its later part.
I examine 2015 through 2024, using the earlier years as context for the adjustment after 2022. The charts suggest an early period of substantial inflation decline with little unemployment movement, followed by a later rise in unemployment. The size of that rise depends on the starting date.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
text:
Data and calculations
I downloaded BLS series CPIAUCSL and UNRATE programmatically with R’s download.file() and FRED’s public CSV URLs. The repository includes acquisition and analysis code, saved data, and replication instructions. Its --refresh option downloads updated observations; the default reproduces the saved snapshot.
Both series are seasonally adjusted. Unemployment is the percentage of the civilian labor force unemployed. Inflation is 100 × (CPI this month / CPI twelve months earlier − 1). An extra year supplies the initial CPI comparison, leaving 120 matched months. Falling positive inflation means prices increase more slowly, not that they fall. Using seasonally adjusted CPI can produce small differences from annual headline rates calculated with unadjusted CPI.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
section: When did the two rates turn?
text:
When did the two rates turn?
Figure 1 focuses on 2022 through 2024. Its aligned panels show whether inflation’s decline began at the same time as unemployment’s rise.








Figure 1: Monthly rates on a common scale. The dotted line marks the inflation peak; points label that peak, the subsequent unemployment trough, and December 2024.





Inflation peaked at 9.0% in June 2022, when unemployment was 3.6%. By December 2024, the rates were 2.9% and 4.1%. That is a 6.1 percentage point inflation decline alongside a 0.5 point unemployment rise.
However, unemployment first fell to 3.4% in April 2023. Measured from that trough, its increase was 0.7 points. Neither baseline is inherently wrong. The first describes movement since peak inflation; the second measures labor market weakening from the subsequent unemployment low.

title: How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?
text:
How did the adjustment unfold?
Figure 3 connects consecutive quarters. Averaging three monthly rates makes the path readable but hides monthly fluctuations. Downward movement means falling inflation; rightward movement means rising unemployment. The horizontal axis is narrower than Figure 2’s, so visual distances are not directly comparable.








Figure 3: Arrows follow consecutive quarters. Quarterly inflation is the mean of monthly annual inflation rates, not an annualized quarterly growth rate.





Choosing an unemployment trough would partly build a subsequent rise into the comparison. Instead, I select the first quarter when inflation completed at least half its decline from the quarterly peak to 2024 Q4. This uses inflation alone. The threshold is 5.7%, first crossed in 2023 Q2. It remains a retrospective rule dependent on the endpoint, not an estimated structural break.
From 2022 Q2 to 2023 Q2, inflation fell from 8.6% to 4.1%, while unemployment moved from 3.6% to 3.5%. By 2024 Q4, unemployment was 4.1% and inflation was 2.7%, a further inflation decline of 1.3 points. Differences use unrounded values, so subtraction of displayed rates can round differently.
Using 40% or 60% of the inflation decline instead gives comparison quarters from 2023 Q1 to 2023 Q2. The sensitivity table reports the results. All three thresholds show little early unemployment movement and a larger later increase.
Unemployment estimates have sampling uncertainty. A change of a tenth of a point should not be treated as a precise population movement. I have not calculated standard errors for these quarterly comparisons and make no claim of statistical significance.
